senses: Square-shaped.
ety: From French quadratique (1765), from Latin quadrātus + -ique (English -ic), form of quadrō (“to make square”), from quādrus (“square”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres (“four”), whence also Latin quartus (“fourth”).

senses: The act of opening or unfolding.
The act of explaining; an explanation.
The sense given by an expositor.
ety: Borrowed from Middle French explication and its etymon Latin explicātiō, explicātiōnem. By surface analysis, explicate + -ion.
examples: Her anthemic "Who Stands For Life" is a powerful explication of what it means to be "pro-life".

senses: A staff with a hooked end similar to a shepherd's crook, or with a cross at the end, carried by an abbot, bishop, or archbishop as a symbol of office.
ety: From Middle English; originally referring to the staff bearer, from a merger of Old French words crocier (“bearer of a cross”) and croisier (“one who bears or has to do with a cross”), ultimately from Latin crux (“cross”).

senses: A style of Japanese animation and comics aimed at a younger male audience.
ety: From the Japanese 少年 (shōnen, “few years”).

senses: Capable of or fit for being smoked (as tobacco, etc.).
Occurring every two hundred (200) years.
Sensationalistic; tending to sensationalize; characterized by sensationalism (the use of exaggerated or lurid material in order to gain public attention).
examples: It was a sensationalist newspaper, even by tabloid standards.

senses: A small flat-bottomed open boat with a pointed bow and square stern.
ety: From Middle English skif, from Middle French esquif, from Old Italian schifo (“small boat”), from Lombardic skif (“boat”), from Proto-Germanic *skipą (“boat, ship”). Doublet of ship.

senses: A dam built in a stream for maintaining and regulating irrigation.
ety: Borrowed from Tamil அணைக்கட்டு (aṇaikkaṭṭu, “dam for regulating the flow of an irrigation channel”), from அணை (aṇai) + கட்டு (kaṭṭu). Also compare Kannada ಅಣೆಕಟ್ಟು (aṇekaṭṭu) with the same construction.

senses: suitable for broadcasting on television
Describes very small particles in a dispersion etc.
A pork dish from the Philippines.
Capable of being saved.
ety: From Middle English savable, from Middle French sauvable, from Old French salvable, sauvable, from Medieval Latin salvābilis; equivalent to save + -able.

senses: Mud from the thermal springs at Battaglia in Italy, used to treat certain medical complaints such as gout and rheumatism.
A writer of screenplays; a screenwriter.
examples: What was acted out in the American and French Revolutions had been thought out beforehand in the writings of Locke and Rousseau, the scenarists for the drama of modern politics.

senses: A tournament in the sport of curling.
ety: Borrowed from Scots bonspiel, from Middle Scots bonspele, possibly from Dutch bond (“league”) + spel (“game”).

senses: choreography
Of a pale yellow-beige colour, like that of wheat.
ety: Inherited from Middle English wheten, from Old English hwǣten (“wheaten”); equivalent to wheat + -en.

senses: To make masculine; to give typically male characteristics.
examples: The global androgenization hypothesis predicts that neighboring males will masculinize both AGD and 2D:4D and, therefore, that AGD and 2D:4D will correlate within sexes.
Surgical interventions for gender dysphoria, according to WPATH, can include feminizing or masculinizing hormone therapy, voice therapy, chest augmentation and reduction, or genital surgery.

senses: To abrade or roughen with pumice.
ety: From Anglo-Norman and Old French pomis (“pumice stone”), from Latin pūmex (“pumice stone”). Doublet of pounce.

senses: A specialist in facial care
In Turkey, a dervish or Sufi lodge or place of worship; alternative form of takya.
ety: From Ottoman Turkish تكه (tekke), from Classical Persian تکیه (takya). Doublet of takya, takiyya, and takyeh.

senses: Foodstuffs that taste very sweet, taken as a group; candies, sweetmeats and confections collectively.
The business or occupation of manufacturing confectionery; the skill or work of a confectioner.
A store where confectionery is sold; a confectioner's shop.
Any of ten former territories defined as homelands for black South Africans under apartheid policy
ety: From a Bantu language (ultimately from Proto-Bantu *bantʊ̀ (“people”)) + -stan (“home of”, suffix of Persian origin), after place names such as Hindustan.

senses: The digit 4 in the NATO phonetic alphabet.
ety: From Middle English four, fower, from Old English fēower.

senses: Ladyfinger cookie.
optoelectronics
Capable of distorting.
Causing distortion, especially in prices.
One who receives a mandate.
One who has sighted or seen something.
A targeteer.
A trial shot in rifle, artillery shooting, or sports like football, to set the range, targeting etc.
A sight on a weapon.
examples: He would have been a great help in the task of examning the reports submitted and interviewing the sighters.
Kane looked in the mood, testing the goalkeeper, Hannes Thor Halldórsson, with an early sighter and then being denied what appeared to be a good goal on six minutes by an offside flag.

senses: A stone marking a boundary in Ancient Greece.
The first step in the bris, where the akroposthion is excised (later followed by periah, then posthetomy, then metzitza).
examples: Milah is ordained in the Bible
The milah (the cutting off of the end of the upper prepuce) is then performed. In medieval Ashkenazic communities it was customary to place the removed prepuce in a container of sand.

senses: A Ghanaian style of music that fuses highlife and hip-hop.
examples: Up the block at Nananom, a tiny music and sundries store, all the hiplife CDs were sold out.

senses: A Jewish aunt.
ety: Borrowed from Yiddish טאַנטע (tante), from German Tante, from French tante.

senses: A person having a hereditary chiefly or noble rank in Polynesia.
A device that carries out carbonation.
examples: But the city now has an answer for that, too: it is offering discounts on carbonators.

senses: In modern style.
examples: The modernistic architecture was both ugly and unfunctional, in spite of its futuristic appearance.

senses: Having the characteristics of a comrade or of comradeship; companionable.
examples: Land must be cleared before there was much stock-work for sheep and cattle dogs. But Bobtails were comradely; they guarded the men from the desperate loneliness in those isolated places.

senses: A spring onion, Allium fistulosum.
Any onion that lacks a fully developed bulb.
ety: From Middle English scaloun (“shallot”), from Anglo-Norman scalun (variant of Old French eschaloigne), from a Proto-Romance derivation of Vulgar Latin *escalonia, from Latin Ascalonius (in caepa (“onion”) Ascalonius, "shallot"), from Ascalo (“Ascalon”), from Ancient Greek Ἀσκάλων (Askálōn, “Ascalon, an ancient port city in the Levant”), borrowed from Biblical Hebrew אַשְׁקְלוֹן (ʾašqəlôn).

senses: Any of several movements in the arts, architecture, literature and music that revived forms from earlier centuries, especially those of the ancient Greeks and ancient Romans.
